newsitem.title: USA: "Funny money" protests end campaign on sour note.
newsitem.headline: "Funny money" protests end campaign on sour note.

text.p: The long, grueling 1996 presidential election ends on Tuesday on a sour note -- loud protests by citizens' groups that campaign contributions from the rich, powerful and foreign have drowned out the American tradition of one man, one vote.

With both major parties having raised an estimated $650 million in the most expensive campaign in history, the big issue in the final days was who gave what to whom and what did they expect in return. Favourable legislation? Access to the candidate? A say in foreign policy?

President Bill Clinton was blasted by Republican Bob Dole and Reform Party candidate Ross Perot for taking money from foreign or foreign-born businessmen with interests in shaping U.S. trade or foreign policy.
The president's men fought back with a refrain that it was legal and everyone does it. Meanwhile they were busy returning checks and tightening procedures.

While Dole hammered at Clinton for taking foreign contributions, saying, "In my administration, I will not sell access to the White House," the public interest group Common Cause reported insurance interests gave the Republican National Committee $400,000 in the first two weeks of October.
That money joined hundreds of millions of dollars in contributions to both parties from all sorts of business and political interests.
While Congress slapped limits on what individuals can donate to presidential candidates, there were no limits on so-called "soft money" contributions to party organisations.
And even though it was illegal for foreigners to contribute to political campaigns, legal aliens living in the United States could give money.
Former Common Cause President Fred Wertheimer, writing in white-hot anger in the Washington Post on Sunday, declared:

"I say without hesitation that this election will go down as the worst in modern times, if not in our history. In important ways the abuses involving hundreds of millions of dollars are worse even than the illegal contributions gathered by Richard Nixon's men during the Watergate era."
Wertheimer said that a record-shattering $200 million in contributions was made "outside federal law."

The Democrats were embarrassed by having it revealed that a visit by Vice President Al Gore to a Buddhist temple raised $140,000, including $5,000 pressed into Democratic hands by a nun who had taken a vow of poverty. She was given the money by someone whose name she did not recall.

Former Commerce Department official John Huang, who raised more than $4 million from Asian-Americans, was under investigation for possible campaign finance violations and for whether he sought favours for his former employer, the Lippo group, an Indonesian conglomerate.

Meanwhile the Republicans and Perot were having a field day with the discovery that Clinton was photographed at a fundraiser in 1993 with a Russian named Gregori Louchansky, whom Time Magazine once called "the most pernicious unindicted criminal in the world."

Perot called Louchansky a money-launderer and a black marketeer in nuclear materials and drugs and added, "They caught him transferring SCUD missiles from Korea over to Iraq. And he got invited to two fundraisers."
Democrats said an invitation to Louchansky to attend a second fundraiser, in 1995, was withdrawn. "He never gave us a dime," a DNC spokeswoman said.
Meanwhile on Monday a new flap emerged. The Detroit Free Press reported Clinton accepted money from Iraqi-Americans who wanted sanctions against Iraq eased.

But the Democratic National Committee called the Iraqi-American contribution perfectly legal and disputed the Free Press story that said $400,000 was raised from organiser Samir Danou and his family. A spokeswoman said the Danou family gave $160,000 but the October event raised $800,000.
The Free Press said Clinton discussed relaxing sanctions against Iraq and quoted a niece of chief organiser Samir Danou as saying the president was receptive to the idea.

The Free Press said Samir Danou, who has lived in the United States since 1965, was a regular contributor to both the Democratic and Republican parties over the years and in the last two years gave the Republican National Committee $25,000.
